**Lemma (B. H. Neumann).** Let `H` be generated by a finite set `S`, let `G`
be finitely presented, and let `pi: H -> G` be surjective. Then `ker pi` is
the normal closure in `H` of a finite set.

*Proof.* Let `F = F(S)` be the free group on `S` and `p: F -> H` the canonical
map. Then `pi p: F -> G` is surjective, so `pi(S)` is a finite generating set
of `G`. A finitely presented group has a finite presentation on every finite
generating set: from a finite presentation `<Y | R>`, add the elements of `S`
with defining words in `Y`, add the relations expressing each `y` as a word in
`S`, and remove `Y` by Tietze moves. Hence `ker(pi p)` is the normal closure
in `F` of a finite set `R_0`. Since `p` is surjective,
`ker pi = p(ker(pi p))` is the normal closure in `H` of `p(R_0)`. ∎

**Proof of the claim.** By the lemma, `K = ker(H_0 -> G)` is the normal
closure of finitely many elements `k_1, ..., k_m`. Since `K` is the union of
the increasing chain `K_i`, each `k_j` lies in some `K_(i_j)`. Put
`i_0 = max_j i_j`. Then `K_(i_0)` is normal and contains every `k_j`, so
`K <= K_(i_0) <= K_i <= K` for every `i >= i_0`. ∎

**Model tests.**
- The family `G_J = <a, t | [a, t^j a t^(-j)] = 1, j in J>` of
  `finite-presentability-two-generator-recursive-is-sigma2-hard`: along
  `J_i = {1, ..., i}` the limit is `G_N`, which is not finitely presented by
  (FP2) there, and indeed the chain of kernels never stabilizes. For finite
  `J` the chain stabilizes at `i = max J`.
- `<a, b | [a, b^j], 1 <= j <= i>` has kernels that stabilize at `i = 1`,
  since `[a, b]` implies every `[a, b^j]`. The limit `Z^2` is finitely
  presented.

**Credit.** The lemma is B. H. Neumann's (1937). The stabilization is
folklore. No novelty is claimed.
